lessons.title: Reading a Company's Funding Mix on screener.in

children.text: Everything in this course so far can be checked on any listed Indian company in about ten minutes, for free. screener.in pulls the filings into one page, and once you know which six numbers to read and in what order, the funding story of a business becomes obvious.
This lesson is a routine, not a theory. Open screener.in alongside it and run it on a company you know.

body.text: A company's funding decisions are recorded in three places: the balance sheet says what it has raised, the profit and loss says what the debt costs, and the cash flow statement says what it actually did each year.

body.caption: The screener.in page, section by section

cells: Market cap, current price, ROCE, ROE
ROCE against ROE is the fastest leverage check there is
Equity Capital, Reserves, Borrowings, Other Liabilities
The funding mix itself, year by year
What the debt costs and whether profit covers it
What the company actually raised or repaid each year

body.label: screener.in
body.description: Open any listed Indian company and keep it beside this lesson. Everything described here is on the free company page, with no login needed for the basics.

children.text: Pull these six out in order. Nothing else is needed for a first read of the funding mix.

markDefs.definition: Accumulated retained profits plus securities premium and other reserves. It usually dwarfs the equity capital line.

children.text: : the Borrowings line, which combines long-term and short-term debt.
: Operating profit divided by Interest, both from the profit and loss.
: Interest divided by borrowings, which tells you roughly what the company is paying.
: the yearly pattern of raising and repaying.

body.text: The Equity Capital line is almost always small and almost always boring, because it is only the face value of the shares. If it suddenly jumps, the company issued new shares that year: an IPO, a QIP, a rights issue or a preferential allotment. The money raised mostly lands in Reserves as securities premium, so a jump in both lines at once is the signature of a share issue.

children.text: Two fictional companies, with figures as they would appear on a screener.in balance sheet and profit and loss, in ₹ crore.

body.caption: Two companies as they appear on screener.in (₹ crore)

body.title: Debt to equity for Company A
body.prompt: Using the table above, calculate Company A's debt to equity ratio. Net worth is Equity Capital plus Reserves. Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Net worth is ₹20 crore plus ₹480 crore, which is ₹500 crore. Borrowings of ₹650 crore divided by ₹500 crore is 1.3. For every rupee the owners have in the business, lenders have put in ₹1.30.

body.title: Interest cover for Company A
body.prompt: Same company: operating profit is ₹180 crore and interest is ₹65 crore. What is the interest cover? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹180 crore divided by ₹65 crore is about 2.8 times. That is adequate but not comfortable: a one-third fall in operating profit would take cover below 2x, which is where many covenants sit.

body.caption: What the six numbers say about each company

children.text: Read the last two rows of the table together. The two businesses earn almost the same return on capital, 15.7% and 15.2%, so they are roughly equally good at using assets. But Company A shows an ROE of 17.2% against Company B's 11.7%. That entire difference is borrowed, not earned. It works because A's ROCE of 15.7% comfortably exceeds its after-tax cost of debt of about 7.5%, exactly as Chapter 4 described. It stops working the moment ROCE falls.

stats.label: Gap for Company B
stats.context: ROE below ROCE, because there is little debt

body.title: Which company would you rather own in a downturn?
body.question: Both companies above face a 40% fall in operating profit for two years. What happens?
options: Both are equally affected, since ROCE is similar
Company A's interest cover falls to about 1.7x, near or below typical covenant floors, while Company B stays above 10x
Company B suffers more, because it has less debt to deduct for tax
Neither is affected, because interest is fixed
body.explanation: Company A pays ₹65 crore of interest out of ₹108 crore of operating profit, leaving very little and breaching most covenant floors of 2x. Company B pays ₹9 crore out of ₹90 crore and barely notices. The higher ROE that made A look better in good years is precisely what makes it fragile here.

children.text: One year of data is a snapshot. The patterns are in the columns to the left.

cells: Equity Capital and Reserves both jump in one year
New shares were issued: IPO, QIP, rights issue or preferential allotment
Reserves grow steadily, Equity Capital flat
The company is funding itself from retained profits. No dilution
Borrowings rising year after year while ROCE is flat or falling
The classic warning pattern. More debt is not producing more return
Borrowings falling and interest falling with them
Deleveraging, often after an equity raise or a strong cash year
Cash from financing positive every single year
The business is not self-funding. It depends on continuous external money
The company is being repriced upward, often after a rating downgrade

body.text: Check the Shareholding tab for promoter [[pledged shares]]. A high or rising pledge percentage means promoters have borrowed personally against their stake, and a falling share price can force sales that change control of the company. It is one of the strongest distress signals available free on screener.in.

body.title: Five things screener.in will not tell you on the first page

children.text: Toggle between them. A parent can look lightly borrowed on a standalone basis while subsidiaries carry the debt.
Under Ind AS 116 leases sit on the balance sheet, but not always inside the Borrowings line. A retailer or airline can carry very large lease obligations that a simple debt to equity ratio misses.
Guarantees given for group companies and disputed tax demands sit in the notes to the accounts, not in borrowings. Open the annual report in the Documents tab.
Total borrowings of ₹650 crore means something very different if ₹500 crore is repayable next year. The annual report gives the schedule.
Banks and NBFCs are not comparable.

For a lender, borrowing is raw material, not leverage in the usual sense. Debt to equity of 6 or 7 is normal for an NBFC and meaningless as a distress signal. Use capital adequacy and asset quality instead.
None of this makes the six-number routine wrong. It makes it a first pass rather than a conclusion.

body.title: Building the base
body.textWithBlank: On a screener.in balance sheet, net worth is the Equity Capital line plus the ___ line.
body.explanation: Equity Capital is only the face value of the shares, which is usually small. Reserves hold retained profits and securities premium, which is where most of the owners' money actually sits.

body.title: Spot the share issue
body.question: A company's Equity Capital rises from ₹18 crore to ₹22 crore in one year, while Reserves jump from ₹300 crore to ₹700 crore. Net profit that year was ₹40 crore. What happened?
options: The company had an exceptionally profitable year
It issued new shares, and most of the money raised sits in Reserves as securities premium
body.explanation: Profit of ₹40 crore cannot explain a ₹400 crore rise in Reserves. Equity Capital moving at all means new shares were issued: the face value goes to Equity Capital and the rest of the issue price to Reserves as securities premium. Check the Cash Flow tab for the proceeds, and the annual report for whether it was a QIP, rights issue or preferential allotment.

body.title: Ten minutes before the meeting
body.scenario: You are in the corporate finance team of a listed mid-cap manufacturer. Your CFO is meeting a potential acquisition target tomorrow: a listed competitor with a ₹1,400 crore market capitalisation. She asks you for a one-page read on how the target is funded, using only public sources, before end of day.
body.prompt: What exactly would you pull, in what order, and what would your one page say?
body.modelAnswer:
What I would pull from screener.in, in order:
1. The top strip: market cap, ROCE and ROE. If ROE sits far above ROCE, leverage is doing the work and the rest of the read is about debt.
2. Balance sheet, last ten years: Equity Capital, Reserves, Borrowings. Compute net worth, debt to equity and the trend in borrowings.
3. Profit and loss, same period: operating profit and interest, giving interest cover and the implied interest rate. A rising implied rate suggests the lenders have repriced them.
4. Cash flow, financing section: has this company been raising or repaying? Continuous positive financing cash flow across ten years means it has never funded itself.
5. Shareholding tab: promoter holding trend and pledged percentage. A falling promoter stake with a rising pledge is the combination that matters most in a negotiation.
6. Documents tab: the latest annual report for the maturity profile, contingent liabilities and any guarantees given to subsidiaries, plus any credit rating rationale, which will state the covenants and the agency's view of refinancing risk.
7. Toggle to consolidated, because the subsidiaries may hold the debt.

What the one page would say:
8. The funding mix today: net worth, borrowings, debt to equity against two or three listed peers, not against a textbook number.
9. Whether the returns justify the leverage: ROCE against the implied interest rate. If ROCE is below the borrowing cost, we are buying a company whose debt is destroying value, and the debt comes with it.
10. The repayment wall: how much debt is due in the next 24 months, since that becomes our problem on day one.
11. Off-balance-sheet items: leases, guarantees, disputed tax demands.
12. Two or three questions for the CFO to ask in the room, such as covenant headroom at the last testing date, and whether any lender consent is needed for a change of control. That last one is the single most important clause in an acquisition of a borrowed company, and it is rarely in the investor presentation.

body.title: The ten-minute screener.in funding routine
steps: Compare ROCE and ROE in the top strip. A wide gap means leverage
Add Equity Capital and Reserves for net worth
Read Borrowings and calculate debt to equity
Divide operating profit by interest for cover, and interest by borrowings for the implied rate
Scan ten years of Borrowings against ten years of ROCE
Look at cash from financing activity: raising every year, or repaying?
Check whether Equity Capital ever jumped, and find out which instrument was used
Check promoter holding and pledged percentage in the Shareholding tab
Toggle consolidated versus standalone before drawing any conclusion
Open the latest annual report for maturity profile, leases and contingent liabilities

cards.definition: Equity Capital plus Reserves on the balance sheet.
Only the face value of issued shares. A jump means new shares were issued.
The amount paid above face value in a share issue, which sits inside Reserves.
Interest divided by borrowings. A rough check on what the company actually pays.
The yearly record of money raised and repaid. Persistently positive means no self-funding.
Promoter shares given as loan security. A high or rising pledge is a distress signal.
Lease liabilities that may not appear inside the Borrowings line but are still obligations.
Group figures versus parent-only. Debt often sits in subsidiaries.

points: The whole funding story of a listed Indian company is free and takes about ten minutes to read.
Six numbers do most of the work: net worth, borrowings, debt to equity, interest cover, implied interest rate and cash from financing.
ROCE against ROE is the fastest leverage test. A wide gap means the return is borrowed rather than earned.
A jump in Equity Capital and Reserves together is the signature of a share issue.
Borrowings rising while ROCE stays flat is the pattern that precedes most corporate distress.
Promoter pledged shares are one of the strongest free distress signals available.
Always check consolidated figures, lease liabilities, contingent liabilities and the maturity profile before concluding anything.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Company A and Company B are fictional illustrations constructed for teaching. screener.in is a third-party data source with no affiliation to this platform, and figures on any data platform should be checked against the company's own filings before being relied on.
